item.title: Scotland’s Flow Country
item.summary: Blanket bogs in the Scottish Highlands store vast amounts of carbon.
item.page_text:
Blanket bogs in the Scottish Highlands store vast amounts of carbon.
Compared to ecosystems in many other parts of the world, the blanket bogs of the Flow Country in northern Scotland are unassuming—soggy, treeless landscapes dominated by hummocky mosses, grasses, and heathers. Yet, to ecologists, the seemingly desolate areas are nothing short of extraordinary.
The bogs store tremendous quantities of carbon . That’s because their soils are so waterlogged that microbes cannot fully break down dead plant material, a process that would otherwise release carbon dioxide. Instead, partially decayed plant matter accumulates into thick layers of spongy, crumbly, carbon-rich material called peat .
The unusual ecosystems, also called blanket mires and featherbed bogs, only occur in places with abundant rainfall, poor drainage, and low levels of evapotranspiration . These types of bogs cover just 120,000 square kilometers (46,000 square miles) globally, less than one-tenth of one percent of Earth’s land surface. The image above, captured by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8 , is centered on blanket bogs in the Scottish Highlands, home to the largest such ecosystem in Europe. This peatland is also the first of its type to be inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site .
The peat bogs of northern Scotland, home to more than 30 species of sphagnum moss , are spread across some 1,900 square kilometers (730 square miles) of the country’s Highlands region. In this image, boggy areas appear dark brown and are sprinkled with lakes. The light green area on the right side around Thurso is farmland. The darker green geometric patterns in the center are conifer plantations . The image was captured in the spring, the part of the year when the land surface is most waterlogged and peat bogs begin to accumulate large amounts of new biomass.
While forests store most of their carbon in living trees—which eventually release it back into the atmosphere when they burn or die—peat bogs often store carbon for many thousands of years. Some parts of the Flow Country have been accumulating peat for more than 9,000 years, building deposits exceeding eight meters thick, according to UNESCO. Overall, scientists estimate that all of the world’s peatlands cover just 3 percent of Earth’s land surface but store more than 600 gigatons of carbon—about twice as much as all the world’s forests combined.

item.title: Oil slicks seen from space : the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems
item.summary: Oil slicks seen from space : the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems. Oil washes up on a beach in Sharjah, United Arab ...
item.page_text:
Since the US war on Iran began in February, there have been hundreds of oil spills, posing a ‘generational’ threat to wildlife
T he vast, dark slicks in the strait of Hormuz are visible from space. Throughout October, oil tankers were struck by missiles or sea mines in the waterway and spilled crude into the sea. The pollution has spread across the Gulf, contaminating coastlines and threatening to cause lasting damage to marine ecosystems that are home to dolphins, sea turtles and countless species of fish.
Eight months into the war between the US and Iran, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes has become a battlefield and the centre of a growing environmental disaster .
The naval blockade of the strait has made documenting the pollution from on the ground almost impossible. But analysis of satellite images, combined with the testimony of environmental experts and marine biologists, can help build up a picture.
The strait of Hormuz, the only maritime passage between the Gulf and the Arabian Sea, is home to a rich but fragile marine environment including coral reefs, mangrove forests and seagrass meadows that support a wealth of marine life.
It plays a vital role in the circulation of water and nutrients and serves as a migration route for marine mammals. Even in peacetime, its ecosystems have faced mounting pressure from shipping, oil extraction and coastal development.
Oil can coat birds’ feathers, making it difficult for them to float and find food. It can cover mangrove roots, preventing the trees from absorbing oxygen and potentially killing them.
Bernhard Riegl, a marine biologist at Nova Southeastern University in Florida, who has studied the Gulf for more than 30 years, warned that the war could cause lasting damage to its confined waters, already under severe pressure from the climate crisis.
“Since the Gulf is shallow, and summer is the least windy period of the year, atmospheric heat is rapidly translated into ocean heat. That heat kills corals, algae, fishes. There is no cold, deep water that could mix and buffer this heat,” Riegl said.
“Everybody knows that oil in water is not good. The potential for additional damage is significant. There is no such thing as a ‘clean war’. Not for the unlucky humans that are drawn into it, nor for the unlucky environment in which the conflict takes place.”
Since the war began on 28 February, Greenpeace has identified more than 500 instances of oil spills through satellite monitoring across the Gulf, the strait of Hormuz and the Arabian Sea. The findings include major spills linked to attacks on vessels, as well as others detected around the time of strikes but whose origins could not be confirmed.
“Adding together the daily mapped footprints [of the spills] gives a cumulative total of approximately 20,000 square kilometres – almost the size of Wales,” said Nina Noelle, a Greenpeace expert on environmental disaster relief.
More than 133 attacks on oil tankers have taken place since the beginning of the conflict, according to Greenpeace. October was the worst month, with more than 30 confirmed or reported attacks in the strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters, according to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. The attacks have continued into November.
Among the most polluting of the October attacks was a strike on the supertanker Gem No 2 off the coast of the United Arab Emirates, which left a slick stretching more than 21 miles (35km). A satellite image dated 19 October shows a huge patch of black moving into the clear waters off the coast of Umm Al Quwain.
Greenpeace estimates that an attack on a tanker in early June resulted in a slick off the coast of Oman that covered more than 600 sq km (230 sq miles) at its peak. Two Iranian naval vessels hit in March continued leaking oil for months, said Wim Zwijnenburg, an environmental researcher with the Dutch peace organisation Pax.
An attack on the Liberian-flagged Minoan Pioneer on 3 August has also been linked to a major slick.
Oil pollution has reached several coastlines since the war began. In March, a slick from the Shahid Bagheri was detected near the Hara mangroves. In April, pollution threatened the protected Shidvar Island, home to coral reefs, seabirds and turtles. Oil was also reported washing ashore at Qeshm Island in August, near important fishing grounds and turtle nesting sites.

Satellite imagery also shows slicks near Oman’s Musandam national park and Iran’s Minab River delta , two areas rich in wildlife. Musandam is home to coral reefs and seabird breeding grounds, while the Minab delta has protected mudflats and forests of mangroves.
Environmental organisations are continuing to analyse satellite imagery but warn that the full extent of the damage cannot be established without investigations on the ground, which remain extremely difficult. Some of the researchers and environmentalists contacted for comment in Iran and Gulf states said they had been instructed by domestic authorities not to speak publicly about the environmental damage caused by the war.
Establishing responsibility is not straightforward, but Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has been blamed for most of the attacks. US forces have also targeted tankers, disabling Iranian vessels attempting to cross a US naval blockade and striking others in response to Iranian missile attacks on US warships.
According to a Wall Street Journal report , the largest oil spill was caused by a strike carried out by the UAE’s air force on oil storage tanks on Lavan Island. The strikes resulted in crude oil flushing into the Gulf and affecting coastal areas, including the nearby nature reserves of Shidvar Island.

item.title: This Map Shows Proposed AI Data Centers Near National Parks
item.summary: This New Map Shows Where. A new interactive map reveals dozens of massive AI data center proposals closing in on America's public lands, from ...
item.page_text:
(Photo: Courtesy of More Than Just Parks)
As America grapples with the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence data centers, two brothers have set out to map infrastructure project proposals nationwide—including those near public lands and national parks.
Will Pattiz is the cofounder of More Than Just Parks , an independent public lands publication that tracks AI data centers. According to his research, at least 14 proposed data center projects are within ten miles of a national park boundary. His data also shows that 38 sites are planned within 25 miles of a national park, and 131 are within 50 miles.
“The basic idea is that a lot of these [projects] are being done under the cloak of darkness or secrecy, and we want folks to know where they’re coming in and who’s building them,” Pattiz, a resident of Portland, Oregon, told Outside . “The stance that we take is that we don’t want them on public lands.”
“Places like Utah, for example, have a huge amount of data center projects and some of the biggest ones that are being proposed,” Pattiz said. “Just depending on the size and scale, they take up a massive amount of resources and will have impacts on public lands one way or the other, whether it’s taking water or the land itself.”
Data centers are rapidly popping up across the United States, fueled by the computing needs of artificial intelligence and cloud-based software. These centers house massive servers, data storage systems, and networking equipment, and they require sizable amounts of electricity and water to run and maintain the hardware.
“The question that we want to see asked is: ‘What is the public benefit from this?’” Pattiz said. “So far, the ones that have been proposed on public lands, there’s no public benefit that’s been outlined.”
To use Pattiz’s map, a user inputs their zip code, and the site shows the closest data center or proposed facility. The site then suggests how the center will affect utility costs, as well as the groups that support the center.
“You can go through that discovery process yourself to decide whether you support [the center] or not, because these are things that are going to impact all of us, and you can decide where you land on that,” Pattiz said.
The map auto-populates as more information becomes available. As of this writing, the tool reflects 2,086 data centers, 741 of which are still in the proposal phase. Of those, 77 are located within ten miles of protected land like national parks, wildlife refuges, and wilderness or conservation areas. Roughly half are in the American West.
In Virginia, 97 data centers are proposed, and 12 are within 25 miles of Shenandoah National Park.
At least 25 data centers are proposed in Indiana, according to the map, and eight are located within 25 miles of Indiana Dunes National Park.
The map also includes several construction proposals that are extremely close to iconic National Park Service sites.
Arizona alone has 26 active proposals, with three within 25 miles of a national park. In January, the City of Page sold roughly 500 acres to developers planning to build a $10 billion data center next to Horseshoe Bend, an iconic viewpoint along the Colorado River. The 500-acre parcel was previously protected for outdoor recreation. According to the City of Page, the proposal is undergoing public review and has not yet been formally adopted, but a planning and zoning meeting is scheduled for November 17 .
According to Pattiz’s map, the center is also located about five miles from the northeastern edge of Grand Canyon National Park near Lees Ferry.
Just outside of Price, Utah, Pattiz found that a company called Valar Atomics applied for more than 9,000 acres of Bureau of Land Management land for data center buildouts, including permits for hundreds of small nuclear reactors, a fuel plant, and nuclear waste storage.
According to a report published by NPR , the so-called Project Beehive would produce about 9.6 gigawatts of power for data centers. Currently, the entire state of Utah produces less than half of that on average, NPR reports.
The land is about two hours from both Arches and Canyonlands National Parks .
Located about 40 miles from Zion National Park , Antelope Data Center is slated for development as part of a 640-acre, 1.5-gigawatt project that will include an on-site natural gas power plant, according to The Salt Lake Tribune . The Iron County Commission approved a conditional use permit in June 2026.
Large-scale data center rollouts represent an inflection point in American history, Pattiz said. As construction crews have erected these centers, they have become political lightning rods in American towns and cities.
Pattiz believes that giving Americans transparent, readily available information about where big tech is breaking ground will help them track what developers are building in their backyards.
“At the end of the day, data is data,” he added. “Whether or not there’s a need for these things is a totally separate question from where they’re being built and what impact they’re going to have on you and the places that you love.”

item.page_text:
Inspired by The Pudding's lo-pi radio , which turns the digits of pi into an endless stream of lo-fi music, I decided to see if I could create something similar for landscapes. The result is The Sound of Music : an experimental map that turns the shape of the land into a musical composition, where the hills really are alive with the sound of music.
The map lets you explore locations around the world and listen to the music generated by their terrain. As the landscape is drawn, notes are played to create a musical interpretation of the contours. You can watch the terrain take shape while listening to the melody it produces. And because the music is generated from the elevation data, different landscapes produce different compositions.
The project began as an adaptation of yesterday's 30DayMapChallenge map. I wanted to take that original contour-map experiment a little further, so I switched the elevation data over to Mapterhorn . This means the map is no longer limited to the particular location and elevation data used in the original version. Mapterhorn makes it possible to generate terrain for locations anywhere in the world (just add a lat,lng to the end of the URL). I also decided to add another dimension to the experiment: sound.
So how does a landscape write its own tune? The map translates different characteristics of the terrain into musical instructions. Elevation helps determine the pitch of the notes, with higher ground generally producing higher sounds. The length and complexity of the contours influence the duration and intensity of the notes, while their position across the landscape can influence where the sound sits in the stereo field. The contours are effectively providing the musical score.
There is a little more to it than simply assigning a note to each contour. The geometry of the landscape is also used to determine the musical character of the composition, including its scale, chord progression and tempo. This gives each location its own musical fingerprint, with the aim of making a rugged mountain range sound quite different from a gentler landscape.
The result is a map that lets you listen to the landscape. Pick a mountain, explore its contours and hear the music that it makes.

Open City · Day 11/30 · Senses: Sound 🎧

Where does Cluj-Napoca roar, and where does it go quiet?

Over Piața Unirii, where three main roads meet, the window roars; in Gheorgheni, between the blocks, the model goes lower. In this 3D map of the city's sound, built in MapLibre and Three.js , 48 km of streets are loud, 84.6 km of railway run beside them, and 83.1 of the 722.1 km mapped are quiet in the estimate.

The challenge: how do you map a sound you cannot measure? I set our road-class estimate next to the city's official noise map, itself a model. In Grigorescu I put the two side by side. They agree on 39 % of residential streets; on 50.2 %, only the official map calls them quiet.
Inspired by Patricio Gonzalez Vivo : the sound haze moves with the noise functions of The Book of Shaders.

What do you hear from your window?

Data: OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL) · official map: Cluj-Napoca noise action plan 2026 · noise estimated, not measured #30DayMapChallenge Day 11/30 #3DMaps #MapLibre #ThreeJS
Geospatial Developer | Real-time 3D Maps, from Raw Data to Browser | React, Three.js, MapLibre
About the data and how this map was built:
🧭 Method: every OpenStreetMap street and railway gets a typical level for its class, lower in 30 km/h zones.
Sound falls 3 dB with each doubling of distance, on a 25 m grid. The streets add up as energy.
The "sea of sound" raises the same estimate: 24 m for each dB above 50, a visual convention.
The haze moves with The Book of Shaders' noise; its shapes are decorative, its color and height are the estimate.
📚 Data: OpenStreetMap roads, railways and runways (ODbL); buildings from Overture Maps Foundation (ODbL).
Official map: Cluj-Napoca noise action plan 2026, strategic map 2021, a model, not measurements.
⚖️ Limits: no traffic counts and no screening by buildings; the 03:00 to 06:30 change is an illustrative profile.
The two maps use different indicators (official: night and 24-hour levels on facades), so I compare categories, not decibels.

item.summary: Satellite image shows an oil spill off the coast of UAE. A satellite image ... An image captured by the European Union's Copernicus Sentinel-2 ...
item.page_text:
Nov 11 (Reuters) - In the Strait of Hormuz, tankers are still ablaze, oil spills are washing ashore and drones and missiles strike infrastructure across the region, despite expectations of a de-escalation reflected in falling oil prices.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported on Wednesday another incident involving a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, while Iran said an oil tanker caught fire after hitting a naval mine.
Reuters was unable to independently verify the reports.
At least 10 ships were hit in the first 10 days of November, after 37 attacks in October, the highest monthly tally since the conflict began, according to data from the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
Videos posted on social media on Sunday and verified by Reuters showed a Navig8 tanker on fire near the coast of Oman. Iran claimed responsibility for hitting three tankers the same day for using "unauthorised routes" through the Strait of Hormuz.
An image captured by the European Union's Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite on Sunday showed a large cloud of black smoke at the same location. Navig8, majority owned by ADNOC Logistics & Services, did not reply to emailed Reuters requests for comment.
US forces have also continued to enforce a naval blockade of Iranian ports. A US military aircraft fired on and disabled a St Kitts-flagged cargo vessel that tried to depart regional waters after visiting an Iranian port on Saturday, US Central Command said.
Attacks in the strait have caused environmental damage, with oil leaking from damaged tankers. A video shared on social media on Monday, and verified by Reuters, showed oil reaching the shores of Oman, while satellite imagery showed oil spills off the coast of Oman and UAE. The Omani government did not respond to Reuters request on Tuesday for comment on the video of oil reaching Omani shores.
Elsewhere in the region, energy infrastructure and civilian facilities have also come under attack. The Iran-backed Houthis have struck targets including the offices of Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company. Video verified by Reuters showed damage to Aramco's office building in Riyadh, following Houthi-claimed missile strikes on November 8.
The Saudi Energy Ministry said that a building belonging to Aramco in Riyadh had been targeted in an attempted attack, with debris causing limited damage to the building with no injuries or fatalities.
The International Maritime Organization has confirmed 133 incidents, most of them attacks, in the region since the conflict began in late February, with at least 25 seafarers killed.
(Reporting by Catherine Cartier in Beirut, Arthur Wei in Beijing and Edward Carron in London; Writing by Nerijus Adomaitis; Editing by Tomasz Janowski, Alexandra Hudson)

item.title: Water Levels at New Mexico's Navajo Reservoir Surge to Seven-Year High - Newsweek
item.summary: Newly released satellite images show New Mexico's second-largest reservoir swelling to a seven year high following heavy rains in the Southwest.
item.page_text:
Newly released satellite images show New Mexico’s second-largest reservoir swelling to a seven year high following heavy rains in the Southwest.
They contrast Navajo Reservoir on September 20 and November 7, after what NASA, who published the images, described as “back-to-back extreme rain events” that lashed the Four Corners region. The reservoir straddles the border of northwestern New Mexico and southwestern Colorado.
The downpours led to a “rapid” rise in the lake’s water levels, culminating in the reservoir hitting its highest level since August 2019, the agency explained. It said Navajo Reservoir stood at 108 percent of average capacity for the date, compared with September 20, when it stood much lower, at 60 percent of average capacity.
The 60-foot water level rise was captured aboard Landsat 9, a joint NASA and U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) Earth-observation satellite.
Southwest Colorado, southeast Utah, northern Arizona, and northwest New Mexico have been hit with widespread heavy rain in recent weeks, NASA noted, adding that the Four Corners saw precipitation totals between two and four times the average from early September through early November. The downpours also led to damaging floods and forced evacuations in portions of the Southwest.
“Rainfall [in northern New Mexico and southwestern Colorado] has been well above average, at times exceptional, during the approximately 3-month period ending this week,” AccuWeather senior meteorologist Alex Sosnowski told Newsweek .
He said weather stations at Durango in Colorado and Farmington, New Mexico recorded more than triple their normal rainfall since September 1.
“Some places in the mountains of northern New Mexico and southern Colorado have picked up three to six times the average over the prior months,” he added.
Lakes Mead and Powell, the first- and second-largest reservoirs in the U.S., have also seen their levels rise amid recent storms .
As Newsweek previously reported, provisional data from USGS showed Powell’s levels rose from a mid-September low of about 3,519 feet to nearly 3,540 feet as of November 9. Lake Mead also climbed slightly during that period, with its levels rising from 1,038.44 feet on September 17 to 1,039.66 feet by the weekend, according to Reclamation data.
Sosnowski said AccuWeather expects above- to well-above average precipitation throughout the winter season in the Southwest. “That includes the all-important above-average snowfall for the mountains,” the meteorologist said. “That then becomes the big runoff in the spring to early summer.”
He predicted that reservoir levels at Lakes Navajo, Powell, and Mead would “ratchet up” over winter, though dips would still be possible as “the winter season can bring stingy periods of precipitation.
“Then, from Feb to May, we should see big surges in lake levels as melting snow and spring storms kick in,” Sosnowski said.
He added that El Niño—a climate pattern that can shift temperature and rainfall patterns—should play a large role during the winter season, with storms likely to pass through portions of the Southern U.S.
“The biggest and earliest bumps in reservoir levels will be closest to the Rockies and will tail off downstream along the Colorado. This is because that water is ‘grabbed up’ upstream. They will release some, of course, but it is a cascading effect," Sosnowski concluded.
As of November 8, Lakes Mead and Powell were 27 percent and 26 percent full, respectively, according to data from the Bureau of Reclamation .

item.title: Some Wisconsin monarchs have made it to Mexico months after being tagged - WPR
item.summary: A map showing a route path with circular markers extending from Minnesota through the central United This map shows Snickers the monarch ...
item.page_text:
After a nearly 1,400 mile flight, Snickers has made it.
And so have David, Nancy, Otto and Bug — just to name a few.
They’re the monarch butterflies who have been tracked by the Southern Wisconsin Bird Alliance since September when they were tagged in Wisconsin. Their migration journey ends in Mexico and new technology shows many of the butterflies have crossed the finish line.
WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter.
Southern Wisconsin Bird Alliance glued 30 solar-powered radio tags onto the backs of monarch butterflies at Goose Pond Sanctuary near Madison. Since then, their migration patterns have been tracked by researchers with the app Project Monarch.
The app detects monarchs in real time. Snickers was detected 944 times in seven  states before crossing the Mexico border.
“There was never really a way to track an individual and see what the migration path is like on an individual basis, so being able to do that on that scale with a whole collection of monarchs is really, really powerful,” Brenna Marsicek, the director of outreach at Southern Wisconsin Bird Alliance, said.
She said monarch migration will continue into December, but 10 of the organization’s tagged butterflies have already made it to Mexico. “This is an astounding distance for a tiny insect to fly. So we have 10 that are in Mexico that have flown that incredible journey,” Marsicek said.
One of the butterflies has made it all the way to her destination. “So Nancy, one of the butterflies, flew over 1,770 miles between Goose Pond and where it is now in Mexico, where it’ll overwinter,” she said.
But 14 of the monarchs haven’t been spotted by the app in over a month.
“They might resurface, they might just be in a really remote part of the country and not pinging against phones, or it could be that they’re dead,” Marsicek said. “Either way, it’s interesting data to know approximately how many butterflies actually make it into Mexico.”
One of the objectives of tagging the monarchs is to improve conservation efforts by increasing understanding of migration patterns. Marsicek said some butterflies flew north to Minneapolis before continuing their journey south. The theory is that this happened due to eastern wind patterns.
“It was just a really interesting revelation that a butterfly would go that far in sort of the wrong direction before continuing their migration,” she said. “It’s been a really powerful tool for us to learn about this species that’s in major decline and needs some really significant help from us to be able to persist into the future.”
Once monarchs make it to Mexico, they rest in the oyamel fir forests, which are nearly 2 miles above sea level and an ideal microclimate for butterflies. Eventually they lay eggs for the next generation to travel north.
The first generation are the offspring of monarchs who overwintered in Mexico. It takes three to four generations, each traveling further north, to reach the northern United States and Canada. The last generation will be the ones who take the long journey south. Monarchs that migrate south live significantly longer than their ancestors who typically only live two to six weeks.
Marsicek said after this year’s migration period ends, researchers will analyze the data to come up with conservation strategies for 2027. She said Southern Wisconsin Bird Alliance is coming up with plans to tag butterflies again next summer.
“It’ll really inform a lot of conservation work that’s done in Wisconsin and throughout the country, as we learn more about what their migration is like and the habitats they rely on,” she said. “It’ll teach us a lot and empower us to help them in the future.”
